# Introduction

This document demonstrates the orchestration of **R**, **Python**, and **Julia** within a single **T-Lang** pipeline, rendered to PDF using **Quarto** and **LaTeX**.

## Data Source Comparison

We consume data generated by three different language nodes in our pipeline.

### 1. Data from R

```{r}
#| label: r-data
#| echo: true
df_r <- read_node("r_data")
head(df_r)
```

### 2. Data from Python

```{python}
#| label: python-data
#| echo: true
import pandas as pd
df_py = pd.read_csv(read_node("py_data"))
print(df_py.head())
```

### 3. Data from Julia

```{julia}
#| label: julia-data
#| echo: true
using DataFrames, CSV
df_jl = CSV.read(read_node("jl_data"), DataFrame)
first(df_jl, 5)
```

## Statistical Analysis in T-Lang

We can also execute T-Lang code directly. Here we use the native `mtcars` (which we'll assume is available or we use the CSV we created earlier).

```{t}
#| label: t-stats
#| echo: true
mtcars = read_csv("src/mtcars.csv")
model = lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data: mtcars)
print(coef(model))
```

## Mathematical Modeling (LaTeX)

The relationship being explored across these languages can be represented as:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - f(x_i; \theta))^2 + \lambda \|\theta\|_2^2
$$

This LaTeX equation is rendered perfectly in the final PDF.

## Conclusion

T-Lang successfully coordinated data generation in R, Python, and Julia, passed those artifacts to this Quarto document, and used LaTeX to produce this professional report.
